appraisal_events.evidence: « Oriane est tout de même encore bien belle ! [...] elle sait bien qu'elle m'aime plus que tant des gens qu'elle voit tous les jours et qui ne sont pas de son rang. » Mme de Gallardon était en effet comme ces amoureux dédaignés qui veulent à toute force faire croire qu'ils sont plus aimés que ceux que choie leur belle.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly likens Gallardon to a disdained lover insisting she is more loved than she is, exposing the gap between her earlier scorn for Oriane's company and her delight at a token gesture.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Je ne sais même pas par quel hasard je sais le nom de ce chameau. Mais c'est la lie de la société. C'est comme si vous me demandiez de vous présenter à ma mercière. Et encore non, car ma mercière est charmante. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Asked to introduce the narrator to Mme Putbus, the duchess erupts into a theatrical tirade calling her 'this camel' and 'the dregs of society,' beneath even her own shopkeeper.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Je vous prêterais un manteau vénitien [...] à la princesse de Parme. Elle chante tout le temps vos louanges, elle ne jure que par vous. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The duc reports that the princesse de Parme constantly praises and admires the narrator, and on the strength of that regard he invites the narrator to join the Guermantes at the redoute, offering to lend him a costume.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mais je ne devais plus jamais, quand je la rencontrerais, recevoir d'elle une seule de ces avances où elle avait semblé s'offrir.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator states that Mme d'Orvillers, who had once given him long, suggestive looks, will never again show him that particular attention now that she knows he is connected to her circle.

status_effects.explanation: Gallardon is sharply diminished as the narrator diagnoses her contradictory, needy performance of indifference toward a cousin she secretly craves recognition from.
Nearly passed over as the duchess heads for her carriage, Gallardon is deliberately sought out and given a parting handshake, a small but witnessed admission into the duchess's personal farewells.

The narrator reads the duchess's calculated, minimal-cost gesture toward Gallardon as proof she fully commands the social maxims of a 'grande élégante,' able to disarm envy at no real cost to herself.
Mme Putbus is sharply discredited in absentia, ranked below the duchess's own tradeswoman and refused any introduction.
The duchess's exaggerated, uncontested comic outburst against Mme Putbus is a display of dominating wit that lands without rebuttal.
The narrator is locally elevated by the reported, if somewhat hyperbolic, admiration of the princesse de Parme.
Being personally invited into the Guermantes' redoute outing, with a costume offered, marks the narrator's admission into an exclusive social occasion.
The narrator permanently loses a singling-out romantic attention he had previously and mysteriously enjoyed from Mme d'Orvillers, now reduced to ordinary treatment.

ambiguities: The narrator's private memory of Mme d'Orvillers's earlier suggestive glances sits uneasily beside the duchess's and duc's later insistence, in response to the narrator's question, that she is not 'légère' but rather 'bégueule' and beyond reproach; this tension is not resolved into a clear status movement for her and is not recorded as a separate event.
